That's really not true at all.

The only sure method is physical destruction or taking the drive out and running it under electromagnets of sufficient gauss. Solid state drives are even worse.

Magentic drives:

The read-write head is normally restricted to the track it writes in at the hardware firmware level. This leaves information that can be recovered from between the tracks, caused by magnetic bleed. Unless you override the way the drive operates on the hardware level you are vulnerable to this. To perform this recovery they take the platters out of the drive and scan them directly paying close attention to the areas between tracks.

Solid State Drives (like the thumb drive mentioned):

These drives contain microprocessors that sit between the OS and the drive itself. These are proprietary, and differ from company to company. The microcontroller handles wear leveling and can enqueue certain write operations (such as deletions) for later. You have no direct control over what and where data is stored on the drive, additionally there is typically some portion of the drive that is only visible to the microcontroller where it can stage and store files for writing later. Unless your tool understands exactly how the microcontroller in that particular SSD works there's a good chance you'll leave some data behind.

Honestly, this sounds like a bluff. If it was erased properly with a multi-pass overwrite, it is highly unlikely they will be able to get much meaningful data from it.

It depends on how good the professional wiping was - if she skimped out and used a company that did one pass with a poorly-seeded pseudo-random generator, then I wouldn't be surprised if the FBI is able to spot the pattern and tease out a ghost of what was under it. This is pretty much the reason why the DOD standard is seven passes - even a halfway competent RNG is guaranteed to destroy the flimsiest ghost of data that way.

ETA: To illustrate how you might see it, modern filesystems keep several backups of their core structures in predictable places. If you know the FS that was used, then comparing where these would've been can tell you quite a bit.

It doesn't really matter if they know the random seed or algorithm or anything. It's not like they're trying to decrypt something. The barrier here is that there was anything at all written over the top of the old data. There's no "teasing out a ghost" from that and if you are aware of anyone being able to do that on a modern drive then you could probably be published.
